chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Jazz obituaries and Depression hardship
summary: Wilson recalls repeated predictions of jazz's death and his own starvation wages in 1929, with leaders blaming promoters for missing pay.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Just like jazz -- I've seen so many

obituaries for the jazz movement. There was one back in the fifties; in the forties when Duke and all the rest cut down the small bands -- you know, Basie went down to seven pieces, Goodman disbanded, and Dorsey quit. Back in the twenties, you know, jazz was swinging during the First World War, the Original Dixieland Band took New York by storm; and then the bottom fell out of jazz, and there was a big revival, and the big band jazz, you know, when Duke went in the Cotton Club and broadcast that jazz, and Earl Hines' big jazz band out of Chicago, and then Cab Calloway came, and then Jimmy Lunceford, Benny Goodman, Artie Shaw in the thirties.

When I got started in 1929, the bottom fell out of the stock market the month I got into it, in October, and the musicians were talking about how good times had been. And I would say, oh? And we starved to death on the road there for awhile, but we still worked. We starved, though, making a dollar and a half a night and then didn't get paid at all -- the promoter would run away with the money, or that was what the leader would always say. He'd blame it on the promoter.
Yeah. What was that thing that Spencer used to do, when they came up with no money at the end of the night, he'd say to the musicians, fellows, you can see for yourself!
Oh yeah. You know, Benny Carter told
me, Russell Smith told Fletcher that when the fellows start jumping on you about money, I'm gonna holler louder than anybody in the band, but don't forget, I'm with you!
Man, that's priceless. Those were some times. We really went through some stuff, Teddy.
